levels.title: Introduction
levels.content:
You are an incident responder tasked with investigating a potential compromise involving the Sofacy group's Fysbis backdoor on a Linux-based network. The Fysbis malware is known to be a modular Linux trojan/backdoor that implements plug-in and controller modules as distinct classes. It includes both 32-bit and 64-bit versions of ELF binaries and can install itself with or without root privileges.

Your goal is to identify and investigate the suspicious activity, determine the extent of the compromise, and take appropriate containment measures.

levels.title: Suspicious Service Discovery
levels.content: While monitoring the network, you noticed unusual outbound connections from the target host. Investigate the target host to identify any unauthorized or suspicious services running on the system.
levels.solution:
To identify suspicious services, you can use the following commands:

1. List all running services:
   `systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running`

2. Check for any unfamiliar or suspicious services.

3. Investigate the service files and configurations for any signs of tampering.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Check the list of running services and look for any that seem out of place or unfamiliar.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use the `systemctl` command to list all running services and investigate any suspicious ones.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: Try running `systemctl status payload-transfer.service` to get detailed information about the suspicious service.

levels.title: Persistence Discovery
levels.content: You have identified a suspicious service running on the target host. Determine how this service is automatically started after a system reboot.
levels.solution:
To identify persistence mechanisms, you can use the following commands:

1. Examine systemd service files:
   `ls /etc/systemd/system/`

2. Check for any related timers:
   `systemctl list-timers`

3. Investigate the service files and configurations for any signs of persistence.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Examine the systemd service files and timers to find any related to the suspicious service.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use the `systemctl` command to list all timers and investigate any suspicious ones.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: Try running `systemctl cat payload-transfer.timer` to view the timer configuration file.

levels.title: C2 Communication Discovery (Port)
levels.content: The suspicious service appears to be communicating with an external command-and-control (C2) server. Determine which network port is used for this communication.
levels.solution:
To identify the network port used for C2 communication, you can use the following commands:

1. Check the network connections:
   `netstat -tuln`

2. Investigate the listen ports:
   `ss -tuln`

3. Look for any unusual or unexpected network activity.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Check the network connections and listen ports to identify any unusual or unexpected network activity.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use the `netstat` or `ss` command to list all network connections and investigate any suspicious ones.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: Try running `netstat -tuln | grep payload-transfer` to filter the output for the suspicious service.
